# Chapter 11: Projections {#sec-projections}

Projection turns a complicated random variable into its closest approximation in a simpler class. In this chapter the simpler class is first an arbitrary linear subspace of $L_2$, then the functions of a conditioning variable, and finally the sums of one-observation terms. These are the geometric and probabilistic operations behind efficient-score residualization and asymptotic linearity in Chapter 25.

::: {.callout-tip title="Why this chapter is here"}

- **Prerequisites:** the [relations among modes of convergence](chapter-2.qmd#theorem-2-7), Slutsky's lemma, conditional expectation, and the central limit theorem.
- **Purpose:** replace a statistic by the closest object whose limiting behavior is easier to analyze.
- **Chapter 25 payoff:** nuisance-score projection, regression residualization, influence-function calculations, and the Wilcoxon example all use versions of this idea.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Companion reading"}

For visual intuition about orthogonality and efficient influence functions, see @fisherKennedy2021, §5.1. For a modern influence-function construction workflow in which residualization plays the same role, see @kennedy2022, §3.4.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Reading guide" collapse="true"}

The route to Chapter 25 uses the first three sections of the source chapter:

- [§11.1](#sec-11-1) characterizes an $L_2$ projection by orthogonality.
- [§11.2](#sec-conditional-expectation) identifies conditional expectation as a projection and records the properties used later.
- [§11.3](#sec-11-3) constructs the Hájek projection onto sums of one-observation terms.

The higher-order Hoeffding decomposition in §11.4 refines the same construction, but its full combinatorics are not required for Chapter 25.

:::

### Roadmap

| Approximation problem | Projection space | Chapter 25 use |
|---|---|---|
| Remove the part explained by nuisance scores | A closed linear subspace of $L_2(P)$ | [Efficient scores](chapter-25.qmd#efficient-score-functions) |
| Remove the part predictable from covariates | Measurable functions of the covariates | [Regression residualization](chapter-25.qmd#example-25-28) |
| Extract the first-order term of a statistic | Sums $\sum_i g_i(X_i)$ | [Wilcoxon local power](chapter-25.qmd#example-25-46) |

## 11.1 Projections {#sec-11-1}

Let $T$ and every element of a class $\mathcal S$ be square-integrable random variables on the same probability space. A random variable $S_0$ is a **projection** of $T$ onto $\mathcal S$ if $S_0\in\mathcal S$ and

$$
E(T-S_0)^2=\inf_{S\in\mathcal S}E(T-S)^2.
\tag{11.1}
$$

The distance is the $L_2$ distance. When $\mathcal S$ is a linear space, the best approximation is characterized by an orthogonal residual.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 11.1: orthogonality characterizes a projection {#theorem-11-1}

Let $\mathcal S$ be a linear space of random variables with finite second moments. A random variable $S_0$ is the projection of $T$ onto $\mathcal S$ if and only if $S_0\in\mathcal S$ and

$$
E(T-S_0)S=0,
\qquad \text{for every }S\in\mathcal S.
\tag{11.2}
$$

Every two projections are equal almost surely. If $\mathcal S$ contains the constant random variables, then

$$
ET=ES_0,
\qquad
\operatorname{cov}(T-S_0,S)=0
\quad\text{for every }S\in\mathcal S.
$$

:::

**Proof roadmap.** Expand squared distance around the proposed projection. Orthogonality removes the cross term in one direction; minimizing every one-dimensional perturbation forces that cross term to vanish in the other.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof</summary>

First suppose that $S_0$ satisfies (11.2). For any $S\in\mathcal S$, linearity gives $S-S_0\in\mathcal S$, and hence

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(T-S)^2
&=E\{(T-S_0)-(S-S_0)\}^2\\
&=E(T-S_0)^2-2E(T-S_0)(S-S_0)+E(S-S_0)^2\\
&=E(T-S_0)^2+E(S-S_0)^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.3}
$$

Thus $S_0$ minimizes squared distance. Equality can hold only if $E(S-S_0)^2=0$, which also proves almost-sure uniqueness.

Conversely, suppose $S_0$ is a projection. For any $S\in\mathcal S$ and $a\in\mathbb R$, the variable $S_0+aS$ belongs to $\mathcal S$. Therefore

$$
0\leq E\{T-(S_0+aS)\}^2-E(T-S_0)^2
=a^2ES^2-2aE(T-S_0)S.
$$

This quadratic is nonnegative for every real $a$ only if its linear coefficient is zero. Hence $E(T-S_0)S=0$.

If constants belong to $\mathcal S$, take $S=1$ to obtain $ET=ES_0$. The same mean identity turns the orthogonality condition into $\operatorname{cov}(T-S_0,S)=0$.

</details>

Equation (11.3) is the Pythagorean identity. In particular,

$$
ET^2=E(T-S_0)^2+ES_0^2
$$

when the zero variable belongs to the space. If constants are also present, the corresponding variance identity is

$$
\operatorname{var}(T)
=\operatorname{var}(T-S_0)+\operatorname{var}(S_0).
\tag{11.4}
$$

The theorem characterizes a projection when it exists. A general linear space need not contain its closest point; closedness in the $L_2$ norm is a standard sufficient condition.

::: {.callout-note title="Theorem"}
### Theorem 11.2: asymptotic equivalence to a projection {#theorem-11-2}

For each $n$, let $\mathcal S_n$ be a linear space of square-integrable random variables that contains the constants. Let $S_n$ be the projection of $T_n$ onto $\mathcal S_n$. If

$$
\frac{\operatorname{var}(T_n)}{\operatorname{var}(S_n)}\longrightarrow1,
\tag{11.5}
$$

then

$$
\frac{T_n-ET_n}{\operatorname{sd}(T_n)}
-
\frac{S_n-ES_n}{\operatorname{sd}(S_n)}
\ \xrightarrow{P}\ 0.
\tag{11.6}
$$

:::

**Proof roadmap.** Use projection orthogonality to calculate the variance of the difference between the two standardized statistics. The variance-ratio hypothesis makes that variance vanish.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof</summary>

Theorem 11.1 gives $ET_n=ES_n$ and

$$
\operatorname{cov}(T_n,S_n)=\operatorname{var}(S_n),
$$

because $T_n-S_n$ is orthogonal to $S_n$. The difference in (11.6) therefore has mean zero and variance

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\operatorname{var}\left\{
\frac{T_n-ET_n}{\operatorname{sd}(T_n)}
-\frac{S_n-ES_n}{\operatorname{sd}(S_n)}
\right\}\\
&\qquad=2-
2\frac{\operatorname{cov}(T_n,S_n)}
{\operatorname{sd}(T_n)\operatorname{sd}(S_n)}
=2-2\frac{\operatorname{sd}(S_n)}{\operatorname{sd}(T_n)}
\longrightarrow0
\end{aligned}
$$

by (11.5). Thus the difference converges to zero in $L_2$, and hence in probability.

</details>

The variance ratio says that the projection retains asymptotically all of the statistic's variation. Once this is verified, a central limit theorem for the simpler $S_n$ transfers to $T_n$ by Slutsky's lemma.

## 11.2 Conditional Expectation {#sec-conditional-expectation}

Conditional expectation is the projection of $X$ onto the linear space of square-integrable measurable functions of $Y$:

$$
E(X\mid Y)
=\arg\min_{g(Y)}E\{X-g(Y)\}^2.
\tag{11.7}
$$

Equivalently, $E(X\mid Y)$ is a function of $Y$ satisfying

$$
E\{X-E(X\mid Y)\}g(Y)=0
\quad\text{for every square-integrable }g(Y).
\tag{11.8}
$$

This is exactly Theorem 11.1 with the projection space restricted to functions of $Y$. As usual, the function is determined only up to events of probability zero.

### Conditional-expectation properties

The source develops the following rules as Examples 11.3–11.9. Each follows either from the orthogonality identity (11.8) or from the defining minimization.

| Source example | Property | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 11.3 | $E\{E(X\mid Y)\}=EX$ | Conditioning preserves the mean. |
| 11.4 | If $X=f(Y)$, then $E(X\mid Y)=X$ | What is already known is unchanged. |
| 11.5 | If $(X,Y)$ has a joint density, $E(X\mid Y=y)=\int x f(x\mid y)\,d\mu(x)$ | The projection definition agrees with the conditional-density formula. |
| 11.6 | If $X\perp Y$, then $E(X\mid Y)=EX$ | An independent variable adds no predictive information. |
| 11.7 | $E\{f(Y)X\mid Y\}=f(Y)E(X\mid Y)$ | A known factor can be pulled outside. |
| 11.8 | If $X\perp Y$, then $E\{f(X,Y)\mid Y=y\}=E\{f(X,y)\}$ | Substitute the known value and average over the independent variable. |
| 11.9 | $E[E(X\mid Y,Z)\mid Y]=E(X\mid Y)$ | Projection onto nested information can be done in stages. |

### Residualization

For square-integrable $X$ and covariates $Z$, define

$$
R_X=X-E(X\mid Z).
\tag{11.9}
$$

Equation (11.8) gives

$$
E\{R_Xg(Z)\}=0
\quad\text{for every square-integrable }g.
\tag{11.10}
$$

Thus residualization removes every component of $X$ that lies in the space of functions of $Z$, not merely its best linear predictor from $Z$. In [Example 25.28](chapter-25.qmd#example-25-28), replacing a regressor by $X-E(X\mid Z)$ removes the nuisance tangent direction associated with the unknown regression function. The same orthogonality is the population mechanism behind the partially linear score and its DML implementation in [§25.11](chapter-25.qmd#sec-approximately-least-favorable-submodels).

::: {.callout-tip title="Three projection operations to keep distinct"}

| Operation | Object being projected | Target space | Typical output |
|---|---|---|---|
| General $L_2(P)$ projection | A score or random variable | A closed linear subspace | Efficient-score residual |
| Conditional expectation | A random variable $X$ | Functions of $Z$ | $E(X\mid Z)$ and residual $X-E(X\mid Z)$ |
| Hájek projection | A statistic of independent observations | Additive sums $\sum_i g_i(X_i)$ | Its first-order asymptotic term |

Conditional expectation is one special $L_2(P)$ projection, while the Hájek projection is another. By contrast, [Theorem 7.12](chapter-7.qmd#theorem-7-12) projects in a finite-dimensional parameter space equipped with the Fisher-information metric. It has the same closest-point geometry but acts on parameter directions rather than random variables.

:::

## 11.3 Projection onto Sums {#sec-11-3}

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent random vectors, and let $\mathcal S$ consist of square-integrable random variables of the form

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n g_i(X_i).
\tag{11.11}
$$

This is a useful approximation space because its elements are sums of independent variables. The projection of a statistic onto this class is its [Hájek projection](glossary.qmd#glossary-hajek-projection).

::: {.callout-important title="Lemma"}
### Lemma 11.10: the Hájek projection {#lemma-11-10}

If $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent and $T$ has a finite second moment, then the projection of $T$ onto $\mathcal S$ is

$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^nE(T\mid X_i)-(n-1)ET.
\tag{11.12}
$$

:::

**Proof roadmap.** Show that the proposed sum belongs to the additive space, condition its residual on each observation, and use Theorem 11.1 to identify the projection.

<details>
<summary>Complete proof</summary>

The right-hand side of (11.12) belongs to $\mathcal S$: the constant can be absorbed into any one of the functions $g_i$. It remains to verify orthogonality.

For $i\ne j$, independence gives

$$
E\{E(T\mid X_i)\mid X_j\}=E\{E(T\mid X_i)\}=ET.
$$

Consequently, for every $j$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E(S\mid X_j)
&=E(T\mid X_j)+\sum_{i\ne j}ET-(n-1)ET\\
&=E(T\mid X_j).
\end{aligned}
$$

For any square-integrable $g_j(X_j)$,

$$
E\{(T-S)g_j(X_j)\}
=E\!\left[E(T-S\mid X_j)g_j(X_j)\right]=0.
$$

By linearity the residual is orthogonal to every sum $\sum_jg_j(X_j)$. Theorem 11.1 therefore identifies $S$ as the projection.

</details>

If the observations are identically distributed and $T(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ is permutation-symmetric, then the conditional expectation $E(T\mid X_i=x)$ has the same form for every $i$. The projection can therefore be written as a sum of copies of one function. This is the form needed for an asymptotic-linear expansion.

### Wilcoxon rank-sum statistic

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim F$ and $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\sim G$ be two independent samples, and define

$$
U_n=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n1\{X_i\leq Y_j\},
\qquad
\psi=P(X\leq Y).
\tag{11.13}
$$

Write $G_-(x)=P(Y<x)$. Conditioning on one observation gives

$$
E(U_n\mid X_i)
=\frac1n\{1-G_-(X_i)\}+\left(1-\frac1n\right)\psi,
\tag{11.14}
$$

and

$$
E(U_n\mid Y_j)
=\frac1nF(Y_j)+\left(1-\frac1n\right)\psi.
\tag{11.15}
$$

Apply Lemma 11.10 to the $2n$ independent observations. The Hájek projection is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pi U_n
={}&\psi
+\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\left[\{1-G_-(X_i)\}-\psi\right]\\
&+\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\{F(Y_j)-\psi\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11.16}
$$

The remainder $U_n-\Pi U_n$ is degenerate: its conditional expectation given any single observation is zero. Its variance is of order $n^{-2}$, so

$$
\sqrt n(U_n-\psi)
=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left[\{1-G_-(X_i)\}-\psi\right]
+\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{j=1}^n\{F(Y_j)-\psi\}
+o_P(1).
\tag{11.17}
$$

The complicated pairwise statistic has become a sum of independent first-order terms. [Example 25.46](chapter-25.qmd#example-25-46) uses this expansion to place the Wilcoxon statistic inside the local asymptotic testing framework of Chapter 15.

::: {.callout-tip title="From a projection to an influence function"}

The summands in (11.17) are the statistic's first-order contributions from the two samples. This is the same structural role played by an estimator's asymptotic influence function in Chapter 25. The projection argument supplies the summands; a central limit theorem supplies their Gaussian limit; and a separate remainder calculation verifies that no first-order variation was lost.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="What is omitted from §11.4" collapse="true"}

The Hoeffding decomposition projects successively onto functions of one observation, pairs of observations, and higher-order subsets. Its first-order component is the Hájek projection above. For the route to Chapter 25, it is enough to recognize that the remainder in (11.17) starts at second order and is degenerate; the general inclusion–exclusion formula is more useful when studying U-statistics in their own right.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Chapter takeaway"}

Projection is a single geometric principle with three later uses:

1. orthogonality characterizes the closest element of a linear $L_2$ space;
2. conditional expectation removes everything predictable from a conditioning variable;
3. the Hájek projection extracts the additive first-order part of a statistic.

Chapter 25 applies the first two operations to scores and nuisance functions. Its Wilcoxon example uses the third to expose the statistic's local Gaussian behavior.

:::
